newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Bahamas polls close as vote reported calm.
newsitem.headline: Bahamas polls close as vote reported calm.

text.p: Bahamians voted in general elections on Friday after four years of relative prosperity seeking a government that would crack down on crime and create more jobs in the archipelago nation.

Lines formed outside voting booths about an hour before the polls opened at 7:00 a.m. EST (1200 GMT). They closed at 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) and the first results were not expected until later in the evening.

Witnesses said the mood was calm, and news reports from the nation's many scattered islands, which lie east of Florida and the Caribbean in the Atlantic, reported that the voting had taken place without major incidents.
Almost 130,000 Bahamians are registered to vote and officials estimated about 90 percent of them would cast ballots.
A grinning Prime Minister Hubert Ingraham, his wife, Delores, and their daughter, Keisha, cast their votes mid-morning. Opposition leader Sir Lynden Pindling voted at mid-afternoon.

In an address on Radio Bahamas shortly after voting began, Anglican Bishop Drexell Gomez read a prayer for peace. He said he hoped those seeking office were doing so "for the glory of your state and not for selfish gain."

Both the ruling Free National Movement led by Ingraham and the opposition Progressive Liberal Party led by the father of independence, Pindling, say they will fight the crime wave and boost employment -- the main concerns of most Bahamians.

The FNM is running on its performance since 1992, during which time it has taken the country down the free market road. It points to its record of infrastructure works, revitalizing the tourist industry, creating 14,000 new jobs and attracting major foreign investment.
The PLP, which was tainted by allegations of corruption during its last tenure, has promised more state involvement in the economy to make jobs.

Ninety-nine candidates are running for the 40 seats in parliament. The two main parties are contesting each seat while the Bahamas Freedom Alliance is putting up eight candidates. The others are independents.

Voters will have their hands marked with indelible ink to prevent them voting twice. Police said they arrested one man on Thursday who was carrying 11 voter cards, but in general fraud is not considered a problem.
At a final rally on Thursday night, Ingraham said he expected the FNM to take 30 seats. The PLP has predicted it will win 24.
Ingraham, a 49-year-old lawyer, was a former protege of Pindling. He quit the PLP in 1984 after opposing corruption.

Pindling, 67, says he will step down in early 1998, paving the way for new leadership. He led the Bahamas to majority rule in 1967 and independence from Britain in 1973, and his policies helped to create a large black middle class.
But his reputation has been badly tarnished by allegations of corruption and he is suffering from prostate cancer.
